theory.intro: Angles at the circumference standing on the same arc are equal. The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on that arc; a diameter gives the special case of a right angle in a semicircle.
steps: Identify the arc that the angle(s) stand on.
Choose the property: double or halve for matching centre and circumference angles; equal angles at the circumference standing on the same arc; or a right angle in a semicircle.
Check whether the central angle needed is the reflex angle (vertex of the circumference angle on the minor arc).
Write the equation from the property and solve. If needed, follow with triangle angle sum, equal base angles when two sides are radii, or Pythagoras in a right-angled triangle.

workedExamples.solution_text:
The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc.
$\angle ACB=166^{\circ}\div2=83^{\circ}$.
$\angle ADB=\angle ACB=83^{\circ}$ (angles at the circumference standing on the same arc).
Both vertices lie on the major arc, so both angles stand on the minor arc $AB$. Their different positions do not change their equal angles.

$\angle AOB=2\times31^{\circ}=62^{\circ}$ (angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference).
$OA=OB$ (radii), so $\triangle OAB$ is isosceles and its base angles are equal.
$\angle OAB=(180^{\circ}-62^{\circ})\div2=59^{\circ}$.

$\angle ACB=90^{\circ}$ (angle in a semicircle).
$\angle ABC=180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-36.5^{\circ}$ (angle sum of $\triangle ABC$).
$\angle ABC=53.5^{\circ}$.

$\angle ACB=90^{\circ}$ (angle in a semicircle), so $AB$ is the hypotenuse.
$BC=\sqrt{AB^2-AC^2}$ (Pythagoras).
$BC=\sqrt{18^2-7^2}=\sqrt{275}\approx16.58$ cm.

$C$ is on the major arc, so $\angle ACB$ stands on the minor arc.
Minor $\angle AOB=2\times67^{\circ}=134^{\circ}$.
Reflex $\angle AOB=360^{\circ}-134^{\circ}=226^{\circ}$.
$D$ is on the minor arc, so $\angle ADB$ stands on the major arc and matches the reflex centre angle.
$\angle ADB=226^{\circ}\div2=113^{\circ}$.
The two circumference angles have vertices on opposite arcs, so the same-arc equality property does not apply.

Let $\angle OCA=x$ and $\angle OCB=y$.
$OA=OC$ (radii), so $\triangle OAC$ is isosceles and $\angle OAC=x$.
$\angle AOD=x+x=2x$ (exterior angle of $\triangle OAC$).
$OB=OC$ (radii), so $\triangle OBC$ is isosceles and $\angle OBC=y$.
$\angle BOD=y+y=2y$ (exterior angle of $\triangle OBC$).
$D$ lies inside $\angle AOB$, so
$\angle AOB=\angle AOD+\angle BOD=2x+2y=2(x+y)$.
Since $\angle ACB=x+y$, $\angle AOB=2\angle ACB$.

Angles at the circumference standing on the same arc are equal, regardless of its position on the opposite arc.
So $\angle ACB = \angle ADB$, even though $C$ and $D$ are different points.

mastery.solution_text:
$OA = OC$ (radii), so $\triangle OAC$ is isosceles, giving $\angle OAC = \angle OCA$.
$\angle AOD = \angle OAC + \angle OCA$ (exterior angle of $\triangle OAC$)
$= 2\angle OCA$
$OB = OC$ (radii), so $\triangle OBC$ is isosceles, giving $\angle OBC = \angle OCB$.
$\angle BOD = \angle OBC + \angle OCB$ (exterior angle of $\triangle OBC$)
$= 2\angle OCB$
$\angle AOB = \angle AOD + \angle BOD$ ($D$ lies inside $\angle AOB$)
$= 2\angle OCA + 2\angle OCB$
$= 2(\angle OCA + \angle OCB)$
$= 2\angle ACB$

$\angle AOB = \angle ACB \times 2 = 70^{\circ}$ (angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference)
$OA = OB$ (radii), so $\triangle OAB$ is isosceles, with $\angle OAB = \angle OBA$.
$\angle OAB = (180^{\circ} - 70^{\circ}) \div 2$ (angle sum of $\triangle OAB$)
$= 55^{\circ}$
$\angle OBA = \angle OAB = 55^{\circ}$ (base angles of the isosceles triangle)

$E$ lies on the same arc as $C$ and $D$, so $\angle AEB$ also stands on the same arc as $\angle ACB$ and $\angle ADB$.
Angles at the circumference standing on the same arc are equal, no matter how many points lie on that arc.
